en: Now I shall explain the treasury of mantras as it was spoken in the Bhūtaḍāmara,
including the sequential method for seed-syllables (bīja) which arises from the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
Śrī Śiva said:
A Vidyujjihvā, Ā Kālavajrī, I Garjinī, Ī Dhūmrabhairavī, U Kālarātriḥ, Ū Vidārī, Ṛ Mahāraudrī, Ṝ Bhayaṃkarī, Ḷ Saṃhāriṇī, Ḹ Karālinī, E Ūrdhvakeśī, AI Ugrabhairavī, O Bhīmākṣī, AU Ḍākinī,
AṂ Rudrarākiṇī, AḤ Caṇḍikā; Ka Krodhīśaḥ, Kha Vāmanaḥ, Ga Caṇḍaḥ, Gha Vikārī, Ṅa Unmattabhairavaḥ.
Ca is Jvālāmukha; cha is Raktadaṃṣṭra; ja is Asitāṅga; jha is Vaḍavāmukha; ña is Vidyunmukha;
ṭa is Mahājvāla; ṭha is Kapālī; ḍa is Bhīṣaṇa; ḍha is Ruru; ṇa is Saṃhārī; ta is Bhairava; tha is Daṇḍī;
da is Balibhuk; dha is Ugrasūladhṛk; na is Siṃhanādī; pa is Kapardī; pha is Karālāgni; ba is Bhayaṃkara; bha...

Bahurūpī (a), my Mahākāla (b); he who is the individual soul (c); drenched in blood (d); the breaker of strength (e); the one with the red garment (f); Caṇḍīśa (g); he whose banner is fire (h); he whose banner is smoke (i); he whose face is the sky (j); he whose nature is the devouring of the three worlds (k). 2. Vidyujjihvā (l), Kālavaktrā (m), adorned by the Mahākālas (n). 3.
The seed-syllable *vi* is the mouth of the Vedas; it is eternal, O Dear One, and is Hālāhala.
Caṇḍīśa, mounted upon blood and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, joined with Nāda and Bindu, is considered the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu’s beloved: *Śrīṃ*.

The first seed-syllable is remembered as *hrīṃ*: it consists of the letter *kṣa* (Kṣataja) situated upon the letter *ha* (Vyomavaktra), adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, and joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
Krodhīśa is mounted upon Kṣataja and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī.
Joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, it is known as *pitṛbhūvāsinī*: *krīṃ*.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, know that [the mantra] joined with *vidārī*, having *vyoma* as its mouth, adorned with *rudra* and *rākiṇī*, is *kūrca*, *kāla*, and the seed-syllable of *krodha*: *hūṃ*. 7–8.
O Dear One, know that the seed-syllable *aiṃ*— which is joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, and which consists of the fierce Bhairavī, the element, and the *vāgbhava*— is the seed of Sarasvatī.
O Dear One, *phaṭ* is known as the weapon-mantra, possessing the great flame of the fire of universal dissolution.
The fierce lord with red, terrifying eyes; this goad (aṅkuśa) is endowed with the sound (nāda) and the point (bindu): KROṂ.
Dviṭha is the head, followed by the wife of fire (vahnijāyā): SVĀHĀ, the beloved of the blazing one, SVĀHĀ.
The fierce lord (krodhīśa), the breaker of strength (balabhit), together with Dhūmrabhairavī, the sound, and the point.
The threefold form is Manmatha, Kāma, the seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds: *klīṃ*. 13.
With the sky as its mouth, enriched by the Night of Time (*kālarātri*), and joined with the armor (*varma*) and the moon-point (*bindu*):
this is declared to be the armor-seed-syllable, O stainless one who delights in the Kula conduct: *huṃ*. 14.
With the sky as its mouth, mounted upon blood, and joined with the *bindus* of the *ḍākinīs*' cries, this luminous mantra is proclaimed as the destroyer of great sins: *Hrauṃ*.
It is conjoined with Dhūmrabhairavī and resides in blood, devouring the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
Combined with *nāda* and *bindu*, the supreme seed-syllable of the *kiṅkiṇī* is *drīṃ*.
Taking the multiformed one (*bahurūpin*) who stands smeared with blood, likewise torn asunder and embraced—this is the great mantra for the specific purpose: *bhrūṃ*. (16–17)
Beneath the smoke-bannered [letter] (dhūmradhvaja) is the Fire of Time (kālāgni), together with upward-pointing hair (ūrdhvakeśī) and the lunar drop (indubindu).
This seed-syllable (bīja), which brings about the end of the eon, was revealed by Bhairava: *spheṃ*.
It is supported by Saṃhāriṇī, while Ūrdhvakeśinī supports Kapardin.
The seed-syllable (bīja) joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, namely *pleṃ*, is known as Vaitālika.
Taking Krodhīśa together with *nāda* and *bindu* while situated in the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], it is called the seed-syllable of Kampinī; Manoharī is said to be expressed by *dviṭha*, namely *klīṃ svāhā*.
Taking up Kapardin, who stands drenched in blood and joined with Dhūmrabhairavī—this is the crow-syllable (dhvāṅkṣa) endowed with the sound and the bindu: *prīṃ*.
Taking up two skull-bowls adorned by Mahākāla...

This is declared to be the *samāsana*, enriched with Caṇḍikā and captivating: *ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. O Dear One, the smoke-bannered [letter] (Ra) situated in the fire of dissolution (E), joined with the bindu (M) at the secret place, and united with Dhūmrabhairavī, is remembered as Phetkāriṇī: *sphīṃ*.
Seated upon blood, with a face like the sky, adorned with a dot (bindu), a crescent moon, and a full moon;
this is renowned as Khadyota. It is joined with Grāsinī and Kālarātri, [the mantra being] HŪṂ.
Seated upon blood, with a face like the sky, and endowed with the resonance (nāda) and the dot (bindu).
Having made the seed-syllable *hrūṃ*, which consists of the essence of Vaivasvata, the ornament of the vidārī [mantra];
[therein are] Vyomavaktra, Dhūmadhvaja, Vāraṇa, and Pralayāgnika;
[she is] Ūrdhvakeśī, mounted upon Kṣata, joined with a bindu and the half-moon. 25–26.

The seed-syllable of Ānandabhairavī, which brings supreme bliss to the mute, is *hasakhaphreṃ*. In the letter *A* is Bhīṣaṇā, renowned as Vidyujjihvā; in the letter *Ā* are Tāmasī, Kālavajrī, and Kālabhairavī.
In the letter *i* is Garjinī, to be known as Caṇḍā Rudrabhairavī;
in the letter *ī* she is known as Śūlinī, the fierce Caṇḍogrā Dhūmrabhairavī.
In the letter *u* is she called Kālakūṭā, Pracaṇḍā, the beloved of Caṇḍa.
Having split [the letter] *ū*, she is called Tālajaṅghā and Kapālinī.
In the letter *ṛ* she is Mahāraudrī and also the Yoginī Jvālinī.
In the letter *ṝ* she is said to be Kālikā, the terrifying Pitṛkālī.
In the letter *ḷ* is Saṃhāriṇī; Meghanādā, who speaks with a fierce voice, is in *e*; Rudracaṇḍā and Kālarātri are in *ai*, and Karālinī is in the letter *ḹ*.
Furthermore, Ūrdhvakeśī and Cāmuṇḍā are recorded as being in the letter *o*.
In the syllable *ai* are Koṭarākṣī, Mālinī, and Unmattabhairavī;
in the syllable *o* are Jvālinī, Bhīmākṣī, and Caṇḍamālinī to be known;
and in the syllable *au* are Ḍākinī, Siṃhanādinī, and Caṇḍabhairavī.
Akrūra, Vidārī, Aṅkāra, Rudrā, Rākiṇī, Śeṣā, Kapālinī, Yāmyā, Caṇḍikā, and the two Kuṇḍalas;
Visarga and Nāda—these sixteen vowels are declared to be Sakalā. 35–36.
Krodhīśa, Vāraṇa, Caṇḍa, Śaṅku, Unmattabhairava,
Jvālāmukha, Raktadaṃṣṭra, Asitāṅga, Balayāmukha,
Vidyunmukha, Mahājvalin, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Guru.
Prahārī, Raurava, Daṇḍī, Balita, and the bearer of the most fierce trident;
Siṃhanādī, Kapardī, the terrifying Pralayāgni, Bahurūpī, Mahākāla, Sthirātman, and he who is smeared with blood. (38–39)
Balabhedī, Raktapaṭa, Caṇḍiśa, Jvalanadhvaja,
Dhūmadhvaja, Vyomavaktra, and Trailokyagrasanātmaka—
these ten vowels are to be assigned in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and heart. (40–41)
When Dhvajinī, Dhūmra, and Bhairavī appear before the eyes, the root syllable is taught as being preceded by *ura* and *mā*; the heart [syllable] consists of the powers of the vowels.
In the absence of the preceding [element], these are applied at the beginning, middle, and end, each succeeding one taking the place of the former.
With his throat and mouth [colored] by Kāla, he is adorned by Mahākāla;
originating from that, possessing five rays, he is the poison of creation, maintenance, and dissolution (43).
Accompanied by Śūlinī, situated in fire, Caṇḍīśa possesses the lunar drop.
This is the seed-syllable dear to Viṣṇu, which is honored and beloved by the world.
[The syllable] KṢA, with the face of space (the letter YA), adorned with the dot of Caṇḍogrā, is the first beloved seed-syllable of Adrijā, Raudrī, and Bhūteśī. 44–45.
Krodhīśa is seated upon red [Raktā] and adorned by Dhūmra-Bhairavī;
joined with the Bindu and Indu, this seed-syllable is known as the melting and moistening [mantra].
Vyomāsya is joined with the Bindu and adorned by Tālajaṅghā.
Kūrcaka, Mahākāla, the seed-syllable of wrath, and Nirañjana;
adorned by Unmattabhairavī and Rudraḍākinī, the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, embellished with the Sound (nāda), increases the intellect. // 47–48 //
"Phaṭ" is well known as the weapon (*astra*); "phaṭ" [is its seed].
"Kroṃ" is the pervasive goad of the blazing fire.
"Svāhā" is the head; the two "ṭha"s are the wife of the fire, the beloved of the flame.
The two right knees are with the Moon; the face of the God is Svāhā, beautiful as fire.
(52) Brahmā seated upon Indra’s throne, the Moon of the Three Forms, and Manmatha are *klīṃ*.
(53) Garjinī and Dhūmrabhairavī are the right and left breasts.
With the sky as its mouth, enriched by the face of time, and joined with the armor-syllable (*vaṃ*), the dot (*bindu*), and the moon (*i*), it is *huṃ*.

(54) The void (*śūnya*) mounted upon blood (*kṣataja*), adorned by Caṇḍabhairavī, and joined with the resonance (*nāda*) and the dot (*bindu*) at the head, is declared to be the Light-mantra: *hrauṃ*. (55)
This unsurpassed treasury of mantras, which was formerly kept secret from seekers and was taught by the Primordial God, has now been revealed by me.
It is the discernment of the treasury of mantras belonging to the Yakṣa-Ḍāmara Tantra.
That which was proclaimed by Krodhīśa to the high-souled Bhairava consists of Vidyuccaṇḍāśinī, Gaurī, Krośinī, Nāginī, Jayā,
Kiṃnarī, Yoginī, Yakṣī, Bhūtinī, Pretinī, and Narī.
She is proclaimed as Grāsinī, Trāsinī, Caṇḍī, and Kālī; likewise [she is known] in Kālabhairava, among all the immortals, and among the Bhūtalāṅgalavarās.
She is Subhagā, Sumukhī, Caṇḍī, Pārvatī, and Suratapriyā.
Urvaśī, Aindriṇī, Līlā, Kaṅkālī, Mekhalā, Śacī,
Māninī, Haṃsinī, Caulā, Kalanā, and Bhūminī—
these are the powers of the first lords as designated by the Primordial God.
Vibhrama, Bāhula, Daṇḍin, Bhairava, Naṭaka, Śuka,
Vṛkodara, Jaṭa, Bhīṣma, Kṣobhaka, Khecara, Naṭa,
Niśācara, Dhvajin, Bhīma, Vicitra, Kauśika, and Yama.
Liṅgin, Vatsādhika, Bhṛṅgin, Maṇibhadra, Ghaṭotkaca;
Mahānandin, Śuka, Daṇḍin, Sugrīva, Kalaha, Bhava; Daṇḍin, Bhāṣāntaka, Ajeśa, Garga, Haṃsa, Pakṣaicara, and Halin. // 63–64 //
That which is known as the seed-syllable of Caṇḍī consists of the garments of the lightning and the Naga women;
in the *aurasādhika*, it begins with the garment and so forth, and this Dhūminī is remembered as the Kinnara.
Adorned by Urvaśī, the swan is extracted from the head of the moon of the swan-king: HŪM. (65–66)
Vidyuccaṇḍā, Haṃsī, Ketu, and Nāginī adorned with ornaments;
Ḍiṇḍibha with blood, Kāminī with dots, and Śaśin with Śrīṃ;
Haṃsagrīvā, Pārvatī, Kapardin, Indu, and others adorned with Hrīṃ. 67–69.
*Krīṃ*, which destroys the life-force of those who desire strife, quarrel, and women, and so forth;
*Vibhramaḥ svāhā* to Raktapārvatī; she is known as Ulkāmukhī.
She is celebrated as Jvālandharī, the dancer (*naṭī*) who possesses the digit of the moon along with the bindu.
Haṃsa and Sugrīva, along with Caṇḍa and others, are proclaimed as Khadyota; [the seed-syllable] is Hraṃ.
(73) This Khadyota, whose body is embraced by Śyāmā, is declared to be Jyotis; [the seed-syllable] is Hrauṃ.
(74) Yama, Sugrīva, Kāminī, Indra, Indu, and others, as well as Kiṃnarī, [are proclaimed]; [the seed-syllable] is Hruṃ. (75)
Sugrīva is also [the seed-syllable] *drāṃ*, which is the fierce Yama, impelled by Nīla and the others with an arrow.
(76) Yama is Sugrīva with the bindu and the moon, the eater of flesh (*piśitāśana*), beginning with *druṃ*.
(77) [He is] the renouncer (*tyāgin*) situated in Maṇibhadra, adorned with the Pretinī and the moon and so forth.
The seed-syllable that brings about the end of the age was revealed by Bhairava: *sphreṃ*.

The seed-syllable of Vaitālika is said to be joined with Bhṛṅgin and a girdle, adorned with Pretinī, the moon, and so forth; it is uttered with *dviṭha* (the letter ṭha) as the captivating *manoharī*: *pleṃ svāhā*.
Vibhrama is Dhūminī, while Caṇḍikā and the others are Kākinī.
Known as the "seed-syllable of the crow," it is hidden in all tantras: *prīṃ*.
Adorned with two *naṭa*s and the upward-haired Dhūminī is *phreṃ*.
Naṭa joined with Dhavānasa, Naṭī with sharp breasts—Ṭaṃṭhaṃ.
Embraced by Pārvatī, seated upon Maṇibhadra, O beloved of the Yoginīs;
she who is renowned as Phetkāriṇī, adorned by Vidyuccaṇḍa—Sphīṃ. 82–83.
The dissolution of Sugrīva’s bones is in the ear; because of its heart-pleasing nature, it belongs to the unimpaired vision.
It may also belong to the impaired one by nature, as well as to Gaurī and Pārvatī.
The root-syllable is declared to be the month; the heart consists of the powers of the vowels.

This treasury of mantras from the *Bhūtadāmara* and *Yakṣadāmara* Tantras was taught by the Primordial God in Jambudvīpa during the Kali age; it is to be understood according to its successive stages throughout the states of existence, their maintenance, and their cessation. (85–86)
For the benefit of mortals, it is difficult to find throughout the three worlds. // 87
